title: Harlem jam session players The Demon and Horse Collar
summary: Early free players at Minton's and the Paradise, and Lockjaw's strictness.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: strict. If you’re gonna play a tune, then play the tune or else get off the stand. “The Demon” would get up there, and everybody else would get off the stand.
There seems to be a history with saxophone players for having this kind of reputation. We know that Charlie Parker in Kansas City would hit those jam sessions…
Yeah, Charlie Parker, well at least he learned to deal with it. He learned to play the tunes the way they were written. He just didn’t play the melody and then go out.

Sure, but I meant in his early period, he was still struggling to understand to grasp the concept of the music. He went on to become if not the greatest improviser, at least among the greatest improvisers. Then, of course, Ornette went on to develop his own language, but what happened to “The Demon” and “Horse Collar”?
“Horse Collar.” I don’t know what happened to those guys. This was years ago. They’re probably not alive now. When they got up there, everybody else would say, “You got it man, you got it” [laughs].
It wasn’t just squeaking and squawking, they were just actually not playing?
There was a lot of squeaking and squawking going on. They were doing the best they could do.
